clips.title: Turkey just tied Greece, to within $25 #Shorts
clips.desc: GDP per person adjusted for prices, 2025: Turkey $45,288, Greece $45,264 (World Bank).

clips.title: Turkey's economy tripled while the lira collapsed #Shorts
clips.desc: Almost 5% growth a year for 25 years.

clips.title: What inflation did to Turkish savings #Shorts
clips.desc: Prices rose almost ninefold between 2018 and 2025.

clips.title: Why Turkey looks poorer in dollars than in real life #Shorts
clips.desc: Market exchange rates vs prices adjusted for local costs.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: In 2000, the average person in Turkey produced about half as much as the average person in Greece, adjusted for prices. {p} Greece, an EU member since 1981, was about to join the euro. Turkey was heading into a currency crisis. {p} Twenty-five years later, look at this. {pp} In 2025: forty-five thousand two hundred and eighty-eight dollars for Turkey. Forty-five thousand two hundred and sixty-four for Greece. {p} A tie, to within twenty-five dollars.

And Turkey did it while living through one of the worst inflation crises of the century. {p} Since 2022, prices have risen by an average of more than fifty percent a year. {p} Since 2018, the lira has lost almost ninety percent of its value against the dollar. {p} Inflation like that usually belongs to countries in deep trouble, like Argentina or Venezuela, not to a country catching up with Europe. {p} So how does a country get richer while its money melts? {pp} <soft>And what does it really mean to be as rich as Greece?</soft>

items.at: get richer while its money melts

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), change since 2000
shots.narration: Start with real growth, adjusted for prices and inflation. {p} Since 2000, output per person in Turkey has grown about two and a half times. That's the same pace as Poland, Europe's growth champion. {p} Argentina's grew about a quarter. Greece's, about a fifth. {p} And Mexico's, a country famous for stable prices? {pp} Up about seven percent. In twenty-five years.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP, constant prices, change since 2007 · unemployment (ILO modeled)
shots.narration: Greece didn't just stand still. It fell off a cliff. {p} Between 2007 and 2013, its economy shrank by more than a quarter, a collapse on the scale of America's Great Depression. {p} Unemployment hit twenty-eight percent. {p} Even in 2025, the Greek economy was still about fourteen percent smaller than in 2007. {p} And as young Greeks left to find work, the country ended up with about seven hundred thousand fewer people than in 2010. {pp} Turkey didn't so much overtake Greece <soft>as meet it on the way down.</soft>

shots.src: Eurostat gov_10dd_edpt1 (Greek deficit 2009) · ESM: €288.7 billion in rescue loans to Greece, 2010–2018
shots.title: What hit Greece
shots.narration: How did it happen? {p} In 2009, Greece admitted its budget deficit was far bigger than reported: more than fifteen percent of its economy. {p} Lenders panicked. Over the next eight years, Greece needed three bailouts worth almost two hundred and ninety billion euros, {pp} in exchange for deep spending cuts and tax rises.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP, constant prices (2000 = 100) · population
shots.narration: Meanwhile, Turkey's economy more than tripled. {p} That's growth of almost five percent a year, on average, for a quarter of a century. Between 2002 and 2007 alone, it averaged about seven percent. {p} And it happened even as the population grew from about sixty-five million to about eighty-six million. {p} More people, and much more output per person. {p} Turkey is also young: about one in five Turks is under fifteen. In Greece, about one in seven. {p} In total, Turkey's economy is now almost six times the size of Greece's.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · Turkish crisis of 2001 · EU customs union with Türkiye (1995)
shots.title: What powered it
shots.narration: Part of it was simply starting from far behind: poorer countries can grow fast by copying what richer ones already do. {p} Part of it was a customs union with the European Union, in place since the mid-1990s, which turned Turkey into a workshop for Europe: cars, fridges, televisions, clothes. Its exports grew more than sevenfold in dollars between 2000 and 2025. {p} And part of it was a huge construction boom: roads, airports, bridges, and millions of new apartments. {p} Istanbul, a city of more than fifteen million people, became one of the biggest economic hubs between Europe and Asia.

Quick favor: if you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} So far, this sounds like a pure success story: an economy that more than tripled, exports up more than sevenfold. {p} Look only at those numbers, and you'd think Turkey had found the perfect recipe. {pp} Now, the part that makes this so strange: {pp} the inflation.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · inflation, consumer prices (annual %)
shots.narration: High inflation isn't new in Turkey. {p} In the 1990s, prices rose by eighty or ninety percent a year. {p} Prices rose so much that in 2005 Turkey knocked six zeros off its currency: one million old lira became one new lira. {p} After a crisis in 2001 and tough reforms, inflation fell to single digits for over a decade. {p} And then it came back. {pp} Seventy-two percent in 2022. Fifty-eight percent in 2024.

shots.src: TurkStat, CPI October 2022 (85.5%, highest since 1998; via Majalla/AFP) · Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye: policy rate 10.5% (Oct 2022), 50% (21 Mar 2024)
shots.title: An experiment
shots.narration: This time, the cause was a deliberate experiment. {p} Normally, a central bank fights inflation by raising interest rates. Turkey's did the opposite and cut them. {p} President Erdoğan argued that high interest rates cause inflation, the reverse of what most economists believe. {p} In October 2022, inflation hit eighty-five and a half percent, the highest since 1998, while the policy rate was about ten percent. {p} In 2023, Turkey reversed course. By March 2024, the rate was fifty percent.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · official exchange rate, lira per US$ (annual average)
shots.title: 10,000 lira of savings, in dollars
shots.narration: So who paid for it? {p} Imagine a Turkish family that kept ten thousand lira in savings in 2018. In dollars, that was worth about two thousand and seventy. {p} By 2025, the same ten thousand lira bought about two hundred and fifty dollars. Almost nine dollars of every ten, gone. {p} No wonder so many Turks rushed into dollars, gold and property to protect themselves. {pp} Prices in Turkey rose almost ninefold over those seven years.

That's the trick inflation plays. {p} The economy can keep growing, factories keep producing, and the average output per person keeps rising, {p} while savers, renters and people on fixed wages fall behind. {p} Turkey raised its minimum wage twice in a single year, in both 2022 and 2023, just to keep up. {p} Pensions, adjusted only twice a year, fell behind month after month in between. {p} Borrowers and owners of property and businesses tend to do better. {pp} Economists call inflation the cruelest tax, because it hits hardest the people with the least. {pp} <soft>Growth tells you how big the pie is. Inflation decides who gets which slice.</soft>

items.text: Size of the pie ≠ the slices

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita (current US$), 2025
shots.title: At market exchange rates, 2025
shots.narration: Now, the catch. {p} Everything so far was adjusted for prices. {p} Measured in plain dollars at market exchange rates, the average Greek produced about twenty-seven thousand dollars in 2025. {p} The average Turk, about eighteen thousand six hundred. {pp} By that measure, Greece is still about forty-five percent ahead. {p} In 2000, it was almost three times ahead.

So which number is right? {p} Both, for different questions. {p} Dollars at market rates tell you what a country can buy from the rest of the world: an iPhone, a plane ticket, an imported car. {p} Prices adjusted for local costs tell you how people live day to day, because a haircut, a meal or rent in Istanbul costs far less than in Athens. {pp} By that measure, Turkey now out-produces China, Mexico, Brazil and Argentina per person. {p} It's even slightly ahead of an EU member, Bulgaria. {p} That's why economists compare living standards with prices adjusted, and buying power abroad with market rates. The World Bank does the adjusting with price surveys run in almost every country on Earth. {pp} <soft>For daily life, Turks and Greeks are now neck and neck.</soft>

items.text: $ at market rates → buying from abroad

shots.src: World Bank WDI · inflation, consumer prices (annual %)
shots.narration: Turkey's inflation is coming down: about thirty-five percent in 2025, after fifty-eight the year before. {p} Still far above Mexico's, at about four, but nowhere near Argentina, where prices rose two hundred and twenty percent in 2024 while the economy shrank. {p} But Mexico is the warning on the other side. {pp} Stable prices, a free-trade deal with the world's biggest economy, and almost no growth per person in twenty-five years. {p} In 2025, the average Mexican produced barely more than in 2007.

The lesson isn't that inflation is fine. It isn't: it quietly wiped out the savings of millions of Turks. {p} It's that stability alone doesn't make a country rich, and chaos alone doesn't make it poor. {p} What matters over decades is whether a country keeps building, producing and selling more. {pp} <soft>Turkey did. The question now is whether it can do it without burning its own money.</soft> {p} And Greece? It's growing again, about two percent a year since 2023, with unemployment down from twenty-eight percent to under nine.
Turkey isn't the only country that has caught a richer neighbor. To see Eastern Europe overtake Portugal, watch the next video. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Turkey Caught Up With Greece. Despite 50% Inflation.
yt.description:
In 2000 the average Turk produced about half as much as the average Greek, adjusted for prices. In 2025: $45,288 vs $45,264. How Turkey's economy tripled while the lira lost almost 90% of its value, why Greece fell off a cliff, who paid for Turkey's inflation experiment, and why in plain dollars Greece is still 45% ahead.
